explanation: Children recited the alphabet ending 'X, Y, Z, and per se and', meaning that the sign & by itself is and. The sign began as a joined form of Latin et.

claims.text: The name 'ampersand' comes from 'and per se and', recited after Z at the end of the alphabet.
The names asterisk, at sign and hash sign do not come from 'and per se and'.
Schoolchildren once ended the alphabet with '& per se and', meaning that the sign & by itself is the word 'and'; the word ampersand is recorded from 1837.
The & sign began as a ligature of the Latin word et, 'and'.

results.title: How the & Came by its Name
ampersand, n. meanings, etymology and more

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The search turned up the 1837 date you mentioned, but the dictionaries give earlier first-use dates, so the answer depends on what you mean by "first known use." [...] Britannica says it was taught as the 27th letter of the alphabet, after z, to 19th-century British students, who recited it that way. Merriam-Webster notes that the phrase was rendered & per se, and, meaning "& by itself (is the word) and." [...] Wikipedia states that the term had entered common English usage by 1837. This is about wide usage, not the earliest written appearance. [...] The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest evidence for ampersand is from 1777, in a diary entry by Hester Lynch Thrale. Merriam-Webster gives 1795 as its first known use. [...] I did not find a source tying 1837 to a first use.

claimResults.note: The recitation half of c3 is supported (Britannica, Merriam-Webster). The year is not: the OED's earliest evidence is 1777 and Merriam-Webster's first known use 1795, while 1837 is only the date by which the word was in common use (Wikipedia). 'The word ampersand is recorded from 1837' is therefore wrong as written.

issues.note: c3's year is contradicted by the OED (1777) and Merriam-Webster (1795). The year is not in the player-facing text, so the simplest fix is to drop it from c3, or to restate it as 'in common use by 1837'. Either changes a claim, which needs two fresh checks (§9.7).
